newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US experts see no Fed move at March FOMC.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US experts see no Fed move at March FOMC.

text.p: Most U.S. economists expect Federal Reserve policymakers to continue to keep short-term interest rates steady in March, a Reuters poll showed.
Twenty-four of 31 economists surveyed on Monday projected no change in the federal funds rate at the next Federal Open Market Commitee (FOMC) meeting on March 25.
Seven respondents said the central bank may raise that key target rate from its current 5.25 percent at the March meeting.

Most experts agreed that the Fed is looking for clear and continued signs of labor market tightness before it will rein in credit. The January employment data appeared tame, although seasonal factors may have distorted the report, they said.

Last Friday, the Labor Department reported U.S. payrolls grew by 271,000 in January compared to an increase of 261,000 the month before. Wall Street experts in an earlier poll had forecast a smaller rise of 237,000.
Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose to 5.4 percent from 5.3 percent in November, and average hourly earnings rose a modest one cent to $12.06.
Mickey Levy, chief economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, said the rate of economic growth is "moderating."
"The pipeline for inflation is more empty than full, despite labor market tightness," he said.
Although the upward movement of wages remains in place, "healthy productivity gains are suppressing unit labor costs," he said.

"Inflation is not generated by a low unemployment rate," asserted Levy, adding that it is generated by excess demand. "Right now, there's not excess demand in the economy as measured by nominal GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth."

For those pundits calling for a Fed tightening in March, economic growth will expand near term at a much faster rate than current market expectations. That, they said, will prompt the Fed to move in March.

"We expect the numbers in the next few weeks to continue to be strong," said Christopher Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc. "And possibly there could be a slight upturn in some of the inflation indicators."
Mostly, respondents said monetary policymakers would wait for confirming data over the next few months before taking action.
John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co Inc, who is calling for a 25-basis point hike in May, said the employment report in January was relatively market-friendly.
But he noted that the the three-month change in average hourly earnings was about 5.5 percent (when annualized), "which was the fastest three-month growth rate since 1983."
"The tight labor market, a lower unemployment rate and continued growth in hourly average earnings" will prompt the Fed to raise rates, he said.
Fifteen experts projected an interest-rate hike in the second quarter or later. Seven said there would be no move in the foreseeable future.
Two economists are calling for an easing in the second half of the year.
Full results of the survey follow.
